# What Convexity Is, and What It Is Not {#sec-convexity}

Part II has established that probabilities are hard to estimate. This chapter introduces the
device that lets a decision proceed without them.

The device is convexity. Its claim is narrow enough to state exactly. **The
shape of your exposure determines whether dispersion helps or hurts you, and the sign of that
effect does not depend on any probability.** You still need dispersion. That is all. You do
not need to know how much of it there is.

## The definition, in one paragraph

Plot your outcome against the variable that drives it. If the curve bends upward, your position is
convex in that variable. If it bends downward, it is concave.

That is the whole definition, and its consequence follows from a piece of arithmetic older than
probability theory: for a convex function, the average of the function exceeds the function of the
average. The gap between them depends on how much the variable moves around, not on the shape of its
distribution.

Turn that around and the practical content falls out. **A convex position gains from dispersion. A
concave position loses from it.** The size of the gain or loss depends on how volatile things are.
The direction depends only on the curve.

| Position | Bends | Effect of higher dispersion | Familiar example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Long options, insurance buyer | Up | Positive | Holding a put |
| Short options, insurance seller | Down | Negative | Selling a put |
| Fixed-rate borrower facing inflation | Down | Negative | Long-dated nominal debt |
| Flexible operator with low fixed costs | Up | Positive | A consultant with portable skills |
| Long-dated commitment to a single technology | Down | Negative | Single-supplier dependence |

The last two rows are not financial, and that is deliberate. The device travels, and the rest of
Part II uses it on decisions that never appear on a balance sheet.

## The two errors in buying convexity

Convexity sounds like a free lunch, and chapter 15 of this book exists because it is not.

**Error one: paying more than the convexity is worth.** A convex payoff has a price, and the price
is usually paid every period rather than once. An option premium, an insurance premium, the foregone
return from holding cash, the salary sacrificed for portable skills. **If the premium exceeds the
value of the convexity, the position is a slow loss with a nice story attached.** This is the most
common failure in retail tail-hedging, and it is not a failure of the idea; it is a failure of the
arithmetic that the idea requires.

**Error two: convex in the wrong variable.** A position can be convex in the price of an asset and
concave in the thing you actually care about. A long-dated fixed-rate contract can be convex in
interest rates and concave in inflation. **Convexity is always convexity with respect to a named
variable**, and the naming is where portfolios acquire hidden fragility.

Both errors share a structure. The device is about shape, and shape is only meaningful when the axis
is specified. **Unlabelled convexity is a slogan.** Nothing more. The naming matters most in precisely the situations where it is skipped, because a position assembled from several instruments will usually be convex with respect to one variable and concave with respect to another, and the convention is to describe it by whichever property the seller wanted to emphasise.

## Fragility, stated as an observable

The negative side deserves its own name, because decisions are usually made by people who do not
have the vocabulary of second derivatives.

Call a position **fragile** if it is harmed when dispersion increases. That is all. Fragility is not
a magnitude, not a probability, and not a forecast. It is a sign.

The sign is observable without any estimate of the future, and the observations that establish it
are mostly qualitative. What is my worst case, and is it bounded? Does an increase in variability
help me or hurt me? Does my buffer absorb shocks or transmit them?

Three questions, no probabilities, and the answers determine whether a position is convex or
concave. **When the answer is fragile, the remedy is structural rather than predictive**: bound the
loss, shorten the commitment, add a second source, hold the option rather than writing it.

## The link to irreversibility

Chapter 11 established that irreversible harm cannot be averaged. This chapter explains why
boundedness converts a fatal position into a survivable one.

A concave exposure with an unbounded worst case is the ruin problem: a single realization ends the
sequence. The same exposure with a bound on the loss is still concave, and it still loses when
dispersion rises, but the loss stops at a number the decision-maker chose in advance.

**Bounding the loss does not make the position good. It makes it survivable, which is a different
and more useful property.** In the vocabulary of the existence grid, bounding moves a decision out
of the Avoid cell and into Bound, where it can be reasoned about rather than avoided.

This is why the practical prescriptions of the fourth quadrant are mostly structural: they do not
estimate anything, they reshape the exposure until estimation is no longer required.

## Where the claim stops

The device has two limits, and both matter more than its advantages.

**You must know that dispersion exists.** Convexity pays when the variable moves. If the driving
variable is genuinely quiescent, the premium is a pure cost. The device removes the need to estimate
magnitudes, not the need to establish that there is something to gain from.

**You must survive the carry.** A convex position is a standing purchase of protection whose cost is paid in ordinary times, and ordinary times are long, which means the practical constraint on convexity is not the availability of insurance but the ability to keep paying for it through the period when nobody can see why one would want it. A convex position's cost is paid in the quiet periods, and quiet
periods last longer than people expect. An investor who cannot fund a decade of premium will
liquidate at the worst moment, which converts a convex payoff into a concave experience.

Both limits are about survival rather than geometry. That is why the next chapter is an accounting device, not a piece of mathematics.

## Refutation conditions

The claim is that shape-based reasoning substitutes for probability-based reasoning in the
direction of the effect. Three ways it could fail.

**If premiums in practice always exceed the convexity value,** the device is theoretically sound and
practically useless. This is a real concern in markets where insurance is expensive and crowded, and
the honest response is that convexity is not always available at a fair price.

**If the relevant variable cannot be identified in advance,** the device cannot be applied. In
complex systems the driver is often contested, and a convexity claim that names the wrong variable
is worse than no claim at all.

**If dispersion is itself mean-reverting in a way that punishes waiting,** then holding dry powder is
not free and the convexity argument must include that cost. This is the strongest of the three, and
it is the reason the next chapter records costs alongside exposures.

## Claim and tool

The claim: the sign of a position's response to dispersion is determined by its shape and is
independent of probabilities.

The tool: the shape diagnostic — convex or concave, with respect to which variable — plus the
fragility questions that make the same distinction available to someone who does not think in
derivatives.

## Boundary conditions

The device applies when the driving variable can be named and when dispersion can be expected to
continue. It says nothing about magnitude, timing, or the fair price of the convexity.

It fails where the premium is unaffordable, where the variable is misidentified, or where the
positions are so interlinked that the exposure cannot be shaped one contract at a time.

And it does not by itself produce a decision. It produces the direction of one, which is the most
that can be had without probabilities.

## Convexity in decisions that are not financial

The device travels because the definition does not mention money.

**A career.** A specialised skill set in a single industry is concave in the health of that industry:
dispersion in outcomes across the sector translates into dispersion in income, and the bad outcomes
are the large ones. A generalist capability set with a portable credential is closer to convex: sector
dispersion creates opportunities as well as losses, and the losses are bounded by the transferability.

**A health decision.** A treatment with a bounded downside and an uncertain upside is convex in the
severity of the condition. One with a permanent side effect and a probabilistic benefit is concave,
and the bounding move — a trial period, a reversible intervention, a second opinion with a stopping
rule — is what converts it.

**A technology bet.** Adopting a standard that others must also adopt is concave in the number of
adopters: dispersion in adoption outcomes produces stranded investment. Running a pilot with a
documented exit is convex by comparison, and the difference is structural rather than a matter of
appetite.

**What the four cases share.** The question is not how likely the bad outcome is. It is whether the
position benefits from dispersion or is harmed by it, and whether the harm is bounded. **Both questions
are answerable from the shape of the exposure, and neither requires a probability.**

## The arithmetic of paying for convexity

The carry is not incidental; it is the term that decides most convexity positions, and it deserves a
worked comparison.

Suppose a hedge costs one percent of the position's value per year and pays out twenty-five percent in
the event it protects against. If the event occurs once in twenty years, the expected payout is about
one and a quarter percent per year against a cost of one percent, so the position is marginally
positive and depends on the frequency estimate being right. If the event occurs once in forty years,
the position is a certain loss of about three-eighths of a percent per year for as long as it is held.

**Three consequences of that arithmetic.**

The frequency estimate matters, and it is the least reliable input — which is the estimation problem
arriving in a convexity position rather than a concave one.

The holding period matters more. A convexity position is a bet that the protection will be needed
before the carry exhausts the resources that fund it.

The cost is paid in the quiet periods, and quiet periods are where the discipline is tested. **Most
holders of tail protection abandon it after a long quiet stretch, which converts a convex payoff into
a concave experience through the exit rather than through the market.**

**What this implies for sizing.** A convex position should be sized so that its annual cost is
affordable from a source that does not depend on the position being right soon. That is a structural
constraint, and it is the practical form of the previous chapter's claim that the limiting factor is
the ability to keep paying rather than the availability of insurance.

## A convexity audit in four questions

The device is applied in four questions, in this order, and the order matters because the first
question can end the exercise.

**Question one. Convex or concave, with respect to what?** Name the variable. If the variable cannot be
named, the audit cannot proceed, and the position's shape is unknown rather than neutral.

**Question two. What does dispersion in that variable do to the outcome?** Help or harm. The question is
about the sign only, and it requires no probabilities.

**Question three. Is the harm bounded, and by what?** The bound may be contractual, physical, or
budgetary. **A concave position with a bound is a cost; a concave position without one is an exposure.**

**Question four. What is the annual cost of holding this shape?** For convex positions, the carry. For
concave ones, the foregone protection. **The cost is what determines whether the shape can be held long
enough to matter.**

**What to record.** Four lines, one per question, with the date. The record makes the audit repeatable,
and repetition is what catches the case where the position was convex with respect to one variable and
became concave with respect to another after a change in contract terms.

**Where the audit is most useful.** Not on financial positions, where the shape is usually known, but on
operational and career decisions, where nobody thinks in these terms and the shape is therefore
accidental. **An accidental concave exposure with no bound is the most common dangerous structure in
this book's material, and it is invisible without a question about shape.**

## Convexity and the cost of insuring yourself

Most people meet the device not as a trader but as someone deciding whether to buy protection, and the
decision has a structure worth setting out.

**The three ways to hold protection.**

**Buy it. Convex, with a known cost.** An insurance premium or an option. **The cost is explicit and paid in
advance, which makes the position easy to evaluate and easy to abandon at the wrong moment.**

**Self-insure by holding a buffer. Concave with respect to the loss.** A cash reserve absorbs the loss and is
spent when the loss occurs. **The buffer's size is bounded by what can be accumulated, which means the
protection is bounded too.**

**Avoid the exposure. Structural.** Remove the activity that creates the risk. **The most effective and the
most costly in foregone benefit, and it is the only one that requires no estimate.**

**The comparison the three invite.** Buying transfers the risk at an explicit price; self-insuring transfers
it to a reserve whose adequacy is unknown until the event; avoiding removes it at the cost of the activity.

**Two errors in the choice.**

**Buying protection whose annual cost exceeds the value of the convexity.** The arithmetic is in the chapter's
earlier section, and the error is usually committed by treating the premium as a cost of doing business rather
than as a price to be compared against the protection's value.

**Self-insuring a risk larger than any achievable buffer.** The buffer looks prudent and is bounded by wealth,
which means it is not protection against the events that matter. **The error is invisible until the event,
which is why the boundedness of the buffer should be stated as a number rather than as a practice.**

**What the device contributes here.** It replaces a question about probabilities — how likely is the loss —
with two questions that require no estimate. **Is the protection bounded, and what does it cost per year.**

## Convexity and the shape of a career

The device's most transferable application outside finance is a career, and the reason is that a career is a
long sequence of bets with a bounded number of irreversible ones.

**The three shapes.**

**Convex. Positive in dispersion.** A generalist ability set with portable credentials, a network that spans
employers, a financial buffer. **Sectoral or technological dispersion creates opportunities, and the bad
outcomes are bounded by transferability.**

**Concave. Negative in dispersion.** A specialised skill tied to one employer or one technology, a
pension dependent on one institution, a household with fixed obligations matched to a variable income.
**Dispersion translates into income dispersion, and the bad outcomes are the large ones.**

**The carry. Explicit.** Convexity costs something: the specialist's premium foregone, the cost of
maintaining a network, the return not earned by holding a buffer. **The premium is the salary difference
between the specialised and the general path, and it is usually large.**

**What the shape comparison does not say.** That the convex career is better. **A specialist who survives is
better off, and the question is what happens to the ones who do not — a question about the distribution
rather than about the individual path.**

**Three questions for the decision.**

**Is the harm bounded?** If the specialist path's failure state is a period of reduced income, the exposure is
bounded and the premium may be worth it. **If the failure state is a decade of unemployability, the shape is
concave without a bound.**

**What does the convexity cost per year?** The premium, stated as a number.

**What would have to stay the same for the specialist path to work?** The mechanism's stability and, where the
path depends on one institution, the institution's.

**Why the questions are worth asking once.** Because the career decision is made once or twice and its shape
is hard to change afterwards. **A concave position with a bound is a choice; without a bound it is an
exposure, and the difference is visible only if the bound is stated.**

## The convexity audit as a portfolio exercise

The four questions are presented for a single position. Applied to a portfolio they reveal something the
single-position version does not: the shapes can offset.

**What the exercise involves. Two columns.** For each position, convex or concave, and in what variable.
**The variable is the part that makes the exercise informative, because positions that look alike on the
return axis can bend in different directions with respect to the variable that matters.**

**Three patterns that appear. Distinct.**

**Aligned shapes.** Most positions concave in the same variable. **Which is not diversification but a
concentrated bet on that variable's stability.**

**Offsetting shapes.** Some positions convex in the variable where others are concave. **Which is genuine
diversification and is usually unintentional, because the shapes were chosen separately.**

**Unlabelled shapes.** Positions whose variable cannot be named. **The most common finding and the reason the
exercise is worth running: a position whose convexity is unknown is not neutral.**

**Two conclusions the exercise supports.**

**A portfolio's shape is not the average of its positions' shapes.** It is the shape of the sum, and the
sum's curvature depends on the interaction of the components.

**The audit's output is a list of variables.** Which is more useful than a list of positions, because the
variables are what a stress scenario should vary.

**How to record the exercise. One table.** Position, variable, shape, bound. **Four columns and one row per
position, which is a page for a portfolio of twenty and an afternoon to assemble.**

**Why the exercise is worth the afternoon.** Because the alternative is a portfolio whose exposures are
described in terms of asset classes rather than variables. **Asset classes are a reporting convention;
variables are what the positions bend with respect to, and only the second determines what helps and what
hurts.**

## The convexity audit and the two-word summary

The audit produces four lines. Its output for a decision can be compressed to two words, and the compression
is what travels into a conversation.

**Convex. Means the position gains from dispersion.** Which is not the same as being safe, and not the same as
being cheap. **A convex position with an unaffordable carry is a slow loss with the right shape.**

**Concave. Means the position is harmed by dispersion.** Which is not the same as being dangerous, and not the
same as being wrong. **A concave position with a bound is a cost of doing business.**

**Bounded. The qualifier that changes both.** A convex position without a bound can still be ended by the
carry; a concave position with a bound cannot be ended by the event. **The two words that matter are the shape
and the bound, and the second is more often omitted.**

**Why the summary is worth having. Two reasons.**

**It fits in a sentence.** "Concave, bounded by the contract term." Which is enough for a listener to know
whether to ask more.

**It identifies the missing item.** Where a position is concave and no bound can be named, the conversation has
found the exposure. **Which is the audit's practical output in most cases.**

**What the two words cannot carry. The variable.** Which must be spoken separately, because "convex" without a
variable is the unlabelled case the chapter warns about. **Three words in practice: shape, variable, bound.**

**How to use the summary. Three words per position.** Shape, variable, bound. **Which is shorter than a risk
description and more informative, because it names the thing the position bends with respect to.**

**Why the compression is worth practising.** Because the audit's value depends on its being asked for in
meetings, and a four-line answer will not be. **Three words can be requested and supplied in a sentence, and
the request is what changes what gets asked next.**

## The convexity audit and the decision to buy protection

The chapter's most common application is a protection decision, and the audit's four questions map onto it
directly.

**Question one. Convex or concave, in what variable.** A put is convex in the price of the underlying; the
position it protects is concave. **The pair is what makes the decision a comparison rather than a purchase.**

**Question two. What does dispersion do.** It helps the protection and harms the position. **Which is the entire
reason for buying it, expressed without a probability.**

**Question three. Is the harm bounded.** The position's harm is bounded by the strike of the protection; the
protection's cost is bounded by the premium. **Both bounded, which is what makes the pair a cost rather than an
exposure.**

**Question four. What is the annual cost.** The premium, as a fraction of the position. **Which is the number
that decides the decision and the one most often left unstated.**

**What the four questions produce. A decision rule.** Buy protection where the annual premium is below the
value of the boundedness, and do not buy where it exceeds it. **Which requires a judgement about the value of
boundedness and no probability at all.**

**What the rule does not settle. How much protection.** The questions establish the direction. **The amount is
a values judgement about the cost of being wrong, and stating it as such is more useful than deriving it.**

**What the audit prevents. Two errors.**

**Buying protection whose cost exceeds any plausible value of the boundedness.** Which is the retail failure.

**Holding no protection because the probability seems low.** Which ignores the fact that the decision's content
is the shape rather than the likelihood.

**Why the audit is worth running before a purchase.** Because the premium is paid every period and the
boundedness is realised rarely, and the asymmetry is what the four questions expose. **Four questions, one
number, and the number is the premium as a share of the position.**

Four questions. Shape. Variable. Bound. Cost per year. That is the audit. Nothing more.

## The audit and the three positions it improves

The four questions are applied to a position. The positions they improve most are the ones whose shape is
accidental, and three types recur.

**A career.** Specialised skills in one industry are concave in that industry's health; a portable capability
set is closer to convex. **The audit's contribution is naming the variable, which is the industry's condition
rather than the person's ability.**

**A supply arrangement.** Single-source dependence is concave in the supplier's reliability; dual sourcing is
convex. **The variable is the supplier's continuity, and the audit's contribution is the bound: a second qualified
source converts an exposure into a cost.**

**A technology commitment.** Adopting a standard others must also adopt is concave in the number of adopters; a
pilot with a documented exit is convex. **The variable is adoption, and the audit names what the position bends
with respect to.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** The shape is a consequence of a decision made for other reasons.
**Nobody chooses to be concave in their industry's health; the shape follows from a specialisation chosen for its
returns.**

**What the audit does about it. Two things.**

**It names the variable.** Which makes the exposure discussable and monitorable.

**It identifies the bound.** Which converts an exposure into a cost where a bounding move exists.

**What the audit cannot do. Change the shape for free.** Both bounding moves carry costs: portable capability
forgoes a specialist premium, dual sourcing forgoes scale. **The audit makes the trade visible rather than
eliminating it, which is the most a diagnostic instrument can do.**

**Why these three positions rather than financial ones.** Because financial positions usually have known shapes
and operational ones usually do not. **The audit's value is concentrated where the shape is accidental, and that
is where the three examples live.**

## The audited position and three questions from a reviewer

A reviewer receiving a convexity audit asks three questions, and they are what makes the audit auditable rather
than decorative.

**Which variable, and is it the one the decision cares about.** A position can be convex in the price and concave
in the thing that matters. **Which is the first question and the one that detects the second of the chapter's two
errors.**

**Is the harm bounded, and by what instrument.** A bound may be contractual, physical or budgetary, and the
instrument determines how durable it is. **A contractual bound lasts as long as the contract, which is a duration
statement and belongs with it.**

**What is the annual cost, and from what source is it paid.** The cost is the carry, and the source is what
determines whether the position can be held through a quiet period. **Which is the question that detects the
first error, and it is the one practitioners answer least often.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each is answerable from the audit's four lines, which is what
makes the audit auditable. **A convexity claim without the four lines cannot be reviewed.**

**Which question is most revealing. The third.** Because the cost is paid every period and the source is often the
strategy itself. **A tail hedge funded by the portfolio it protects is not a hedge through a drawdown, and the
question exposes it in one sentence.**

**How to record the answers. Three clauses per position.** Variable, bound and instrument, cost and source.
**Which is one line and which is the whole of what a reviewer needs.**

**Why the three questions are worth stating.** Because convexity is discussed as a property and reviewed as a
position. **Three questions, answerable from four lines, and the difference between a property and a position is
what a reviewer is for.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The mathematics is standard. The classification of positions, the three fragility questions, and the
statement that bounding converts a ruin problem into a bounded one are the book's presentation, and
the last of these is argued rather than demonstrated — I know of no empirical study that measures
whether practitioners who use the sign diagnostic make better decisions than those who do not.
